summary: Specifies protocol extensions for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering, which lets bandwidth be reserved separately per class of traffic. It generalizes existing routing-protocol extensions from RFC 3630 and RFC 3784, adds some new ones, and extends RSVP-TE signaling. This is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A highway can set aside one lane for ambulances and another for regular cars. This memo teaches network routers to keep track of separate bandwidth for different kinds of traffic so important data always has room.

questions: what is diffserv-aware mpls traffic engineering
what is a te-class in mpls
what is the classtype object in rsvp-te
subtitle: How MPLS traffic engineering learns to reserve bandwidth separately for each class of traffic, such as voice and data.

tldr.problem: Existing MPLS traffic engineering reserves bandwidth as one pool, so a provider cannot enforce different bandwidth limits for different classes of traffic, such as voice and data.
tldr.mechanism: Traffic is grouped into up to 8 Class-Types, each with its own bandwidth constraints. Pairs of Class-Type and preemption priority form TE-Classes, which the IGP advertises and RSVP-TE signals with a new CLASSTYPE object.
tldr.outcome: Routers can place each LSP using the bandwidth left for its own class, and ordinary MPLS TE is just the special case with one Class-Type.

today: RFC 4124 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DS-TE Needs New Protocol Support
sections.content:
RFC 4124 specifies the protocol extensions for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE). The requirement it serves, taken from RFC 3564, is the ability to enforce different bandwidth constraints for different classes of traffic. The document extends the routing-protocol (IGP) and RSVP-TE signaling already defined for MPLS Traffic Engineering, and it works with distributed Constraint-Based Routing, where head-end routers compute paths.

It does not pick a particular Bandwidth Constraints model. The extensions do support the Russian Dolls Model, the Maximum Allocation Model and the Maximum Allocation with Reservation Model, though the RFC says they may not suffice for every conceivable model.

The RFC also notes how DS-TE differs from plain Diffserv. Diffserv does not indicate preemption, while DS-TE has multiple levels of preemption for its Class-Types. Diffserv has no way to control overbooking explicitly, while DS-TE allows it.
sections.eli5: Normal traffic engineering gives every car the same road budget. This memo lets the road planners keep a separate budget for ambulances, buses and cars.

sections.title: Class-Types, Traffic Trunks and TE-Classes
sections.content:
A Traffic Trunk is an aggregation of traffic flows of the same class placed inside a Label Switched Path (LSP). A Class-Type (CT) is the set of Traffic Trunks crossing a link that is governed by a specific set of bandwidth constraints. A given Traffic Trunk belongs to the same CT on all links.

A TE-Class is a pair of a Class-Type and a preemption priority allowed for that Class-Type. An LSP of that Class-Type can use the priority as its setup priority, holding priority, or both.

Each link can have up to 8 Bandwidth Constraints (BC0 to BC7). The existing Maximum Reservable Bandwidth keeps its name but now means the aggregate constraint across all Class-Types, so the sum of reserved bandwidth over CT0 to CT7 must not exceed it.
sections.eli5: A Class-Type is a team of traffic, like the buses. A TE-Class is the team plus how important it is allowed to be when roads get full.

sections.title: Configuring Links, Routers and LSPs
sections.content:
A DS-TE router MUST allow up to 8 BCs per link and MUST interpret them according to the Bandwidth Constraints model in use. If the model imposes a relationship between the values, the router MUST enforce it at configuration time. With the Russian Dolls model, for example, BCi must be smaller than or equal to BCj when i is greater than j, and BC0 must equal the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth.

Each router MUST allow a TE-Class mapping for up to 8 TE-Classes, written TE-Class[i] <--> < CTc, preemption p >. Two TE-Classes MUST NOT be identical, unused entries may be marked Unused, and the same mapping MUST be configured on every router in the DS-TE domain. During a change of mapping, the RFC recommends that active tunnels avoid the TE-Classes being modified.

Each LSP gets exactly one Class-Type plus setup and holding priorities from 0 to 7. The Class-Type with the setup priority, and the Class-Type with the holding priority, MUST each form a configured TE-Class, and the router MUST enforce this at configuration time.

For overbooking, the RFC describes two methods that need no extra parameters: LSP Size Overbooking and Link Size Overbooking.
sections.eli5: Before anything works, every router gets the same rule book that says which teams exist and how important each one can be. Every tunnel must pick a team and an importance that is in the rule book.

sections.title: Worked Configuration Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives five examples, all using CT1 for Voice and CT0 for Data. In Example 1 the mapping is TE-Class[0] = <CT1, preemption 0> and TE-Class[1] = <CT0, preemption 1>. Voice LSPs use setup and holding priority 0 and Data LSPs use 1. A new Voice LSP can preempt an existing Data LSP, but a Data LSP never preempts a Voice LSP.

Example 4 maps both CT1 and CT0 to preemption 0, so that no LSP can preempt any other. The other examples split Voice and Data further into large and small LSPs, or limit preemption for network stability, by choosing different priorities.
sections.eli5: By picking who gets the high-priority badge, a network owner decides whether voice can bump data out of the way, or whether nobody bumps anybody.

sections.title: IGP Extensions: Bandwidth Constraints and Unreserved Bandwidth
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new optional Bandwidth Constraints sub-TLV: a 1-octet Bandwidth Constraints Model Id, 3 reserved octets, then N x 4 octets of BC values. Each BC is a 32-bit IEEE floating point number in bytes (not bits) per second. In OSPF it is a sub-TLV of the Link TLV with type 17; in IS-IS it is a sub-TLV of the extended IS reachability TLV with type 22. Advertising BCs is optional, but a router that does so MUST use this sub-TLV alongside the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth sub-TLV.

A router that receives a Model Id different from the one it uses SHOULD warn the operator. It MAY discard the TLV if it does not support that model or cannot run several models at once.

The existing Unreserved Bandwidth sub-TLV stays the only carrier of dynamic bandwidth information, but its eight values now correspond to TE-Classes 0 to 7 instead of preemption priorities. A router MUST NOT assume the values are ordered, because different Class-Types have different constraints. Unused TE-Classes are advertised as zero and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: Each router tells its neighbours how much room is left in each team's budget. The numbers do not have to shrink from top to bottom any more, because every team has its own budget.

sections.title: RSVP-TE Signaling, Path Computation and Admission
sections.content:
A new optional RSVP object, CLASSTYPE (Class Number 66, C-Type 1), appears in Path messages that set up LSP tunnels. It holds 29 reserved bits and a 3-bit CT field, with values 1 to 7 allowed and 0 reserved. For Class-Type 0 the sender MUST NOT include it, which keeps compatibility with routers that are not DS-TE capable. If it is absent, the router treats the LSP as Class-Type 0. Each router on the path records the object, and the Resv message MUST NOT carry one.

A router performs admission control against the bandwidth available for that Class-Type. An LSP of bandwidth B, setup priority p and Class-Type CTc is admissible if and only if B is less than or equal to the Unreserved Bandwidth for the TE-Class that maps to CTc and p. The RFC leaves the actual admission algorithm to vendors but requires the advertised values to reflect all relevant BCs and to use the holding priority of established LSPs.

Path computation needs no new algorithm: a head-end only has to fit the LSP into the single value Unreserved TE-Class[i] on each link. The BCs may optionally serve as a tie-breaker. The Class-Type MAY also be used to adjust the Diffserv scheduler.
sections.eli5: When a router asks for a tunnel, it writes the team name on the request. Each router on the way checks that team's budget and says yes only if the tunnel fits.

sections.title: Error Reporting
sections.content:
Problems with a CLASSTYPE object are reported with a PathErr carrying the new RSVP error code 28, "Diffserv-aware TE Error". The error values are:

  • 1 Unexpected CLASSTYPE object, for a Path message without a LABEL_REQUEST object or the LSP_Tunnel_IPv4 session type
  • 2 Unsupported Class-Type
  • 3 Invalid Class-Type value, meaning 0
  • 4, 5 and 6 when the Class-Type and the setup priority, the holding priority, or both, do not form a configured TE-Class
  • 7 and 8 when the signaled PSC or PHBs are inconsistent with the Class-Type

A router that does not recognize the CLASSTYPE object follows the normal RSVP rules for unknown objects and sends a PathErr, so the setup fails. The sender SHOULD notify the operator and might retry without the CLASSTYPE object.
sections.eli5: If the request has the wrong team name or a badge that is not in the rule book, the router sends the request back with a note saying what was wrong.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Existing TE is a special case of DS-TE: one Class-Type (CT0), all 8 preemption priorities allowed, and the mapping TE-Class[i] = <CT0, preemption i>. In that case DS-TE behaves as existing TE and no Class-Type is signaled. In a mixed network, Appendix C requires the DS-TE domain to have a CT0 TE-Class for each preemption priority used in the TE domain, with the index equal to the preemption priority.

On security, the document introduces no additional threats beyond those of Diffserv and MPLS Traffic Engineering, and the same measures apply. It stresses that changing administratively configured parameters, such as those for DS-TE LSPs, must be done securely by authorized entities.
sections.eli5: An old-style network is just a new-style network with only one team, so old and new routers can be mixed. The usual locks that protect the network still apply.

fields.desc: Bandwidth Constraints Model in use by the advertising router.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero on send and ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: 32-bit IEEE float in bytes per second; BC1 onward follow, each 4 octets.

fields.desc: MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: Class-Type; values 1 to 7 are allowed and 0 is reserved.
